title: The Rep Has a Range, Not a Ruler
subtitle: Fuller movement is often a useful starting point for strength training. The goal is a controlled, repeatable range that works for the person doing the rep—not a matching pose.

body: A range is a choice, not a standard

A repetition has a beginning, an end, and the path between them. In training, range of motion describes how far a joint or body segment moves during that repetition. “Full range” is useful shorthand for moving through a broad, controlled portion of the available motion. It does not mean forcing a joint to its furthest possible endpoint, nor does it require every person to reach the same depth or position.

That distinction matters because bodies differ in proportions, joint structure, experience, balance, and the movement being trained. Two people can perform the same exercise with different visible endpoints and still use a deliberate, repeatable range. The question is not whether your squat looks like someone else’s. It is whether you can control the movement you chose, repeat it consistently, and adjust it when the exercise or your circumstances call for a change.
What the evidence says—and what it doesn’t

A 2026 American College of Sports Medicine position stand synthesizing 137 systematic reviews and more than 30,000 participants found full range of motion among the resistance-training variables associated with improved strength. That supports using a broad, controlled range as a useful default, but it does not establish one identical range for every person or exercise [1].

A 2021 review of 16 studies found greater strength and lower-limb muscle growth with full-range than partial-range training; results for functional performance favored full range but were not statistically significant [2]. Muscle growth, or hypertrophy, has a more varied picture. A separate review of 11 studies found that outcomes differed by muscle and by which portion of the range was trained; some partial-range approaches did well for particular growth outcomes [3].

These findings are not contradictory so much as specific. Strength, muscle growth, and everyday performance are different outcomes, and a result for one does not automatically settle the others. The practical takeaway is neither “always go deeper” nor “partials are better.” Start with a controlled range that suits the movement, then make a deliberate choice about whether to change it.
Why two good reps may look different

In a squat, for example, one person may lower until their thighs are near parallel while another stops higher. The visible difference could reflect limb proportions, balance, the exercise setup, or simply a different range that each can control. Depth alone does not tell you how much effort a rep required or whether its motion was repeatable.

The same principle applies to a push-up, row, split squat, or resistance-band press. A push-up from a wall or bench uses a different path than one from the floor; both can be ways to load the pushing muscles. A row may finish when the upper arm reaches the torso rather than when the shoulder is pulled as far back as possible. In each case, the endpoint should be a chosen part of the exercise—not a place you reach by bouncing, twisting, or losing control.

Range is adjustable training information. It is not a score for flexibility, toughness, or worth. That makes it possible to train with a partner without turning their body into a template for yours.
Find a repeatable range in three passes

Try this with a light load or a body-weight version before adding difficulty. First, set up the movement: choose a stable stance or support, place your equipment, and decide where the rep will begin. Then perform a few slow, comfortable repetitions, moving only as far as you can stay balanced and in control. Notice where the movement starts to change—perhaps your heel lifts, your trunk shifts, or the weight drifts away from its intended path.

Next, choose a clear endpoint just before that change, rather than trying to push past it. Repeat several reps to see whether you can arrive there consistently. If the endpoint varies widely, make the range a little smaller or use a simpler version, such as a chair-assisted squat or a wall push-up. Finally, record the setup and endpoint in plain language: “lower until lightly touching the bench” or “bring the band to the ribs without leaning back.”

This is a way to organize general training, not a test or a rehabilitation plan. Don’t force a painful or unstable position to satisfy an idea of full range. If a movement raises a concern you cannot resolve by changing the setup or choosing another exercise, seek individualized guidance from an appropriate professional.
Use the exercise to make the range workable

A range is shaped by the exercise, not just by the person. Changing the load, support, or starting position can make a movement easier to control. For a squat, sit to a chair or bench and stand again; as the movement becomes familiar, the target can be lowered if that remains comfortable and steady. For a split squat, a hand on a wall or sturdy support can make balance less of a limiting factor. With a band row, stepping closer or farther from the anchor changes resistance, while a small adjustment in stance can help keep the torso quiet.

These options are not lesser versions reserved for beginners. They are ways to choose the demand you want to practice. A movement should fit the space and equipment available, and its range should be one you can reproduce there.
Track the movement, not someone else’s depth

To see whether your chosen range is consistent, use one simple cue or marker. A chair gives a squat a touchpoint; a wall or bench sets the height for an incline push-up; a band’s anchor and your stance help make a row repeatable. Keep the same setup across a set, and notice whether the final repetitions still follow the path you intended. If form changes sharply as fatigue builds, shorten the set or reduce the load rather than reaching for a bigger range by sacrificing control.

If you train with a friend, agree to compare notes rather than positions. One person might say, “I can reach the bench without shifting my feet,” while the other says, “I’m stopping above it and staying steady.” Both observations can help each person decide what to repeat next time. A brief note—exercise, setup, range cue, load—can also make progression easier to judge. Progress might mean a steadier rep, a little more range, or a modest increase in resistance; it does not have to mean all three at once.
Let the range change when the reason changes

A consistent range makes it easier to compare today’s reps with last week’s. Consistency does not mean that range is fixed forever. A different exercise, load, support, surface, or level of fatigue can change what you can control. If you deliberately alter the endpoint, note that change so you do not mistake a deeper movement for an increase in strength under otherwise identical conditions.

Full range is a useful starting point because research often finds benefits for strength, and in some settings for muscle growth. But a range that is shorter and controlled can still be a sensible way to train, particularly when the goal, exercise, or available setup calls for it. Keep the decision concrete: choose a movement, set an endpoint you can repeat, and check whether it remains comfortable and stable. The best rep is not the one that reaches the farthest. It is the one whose range makes sense for the training you are doing.
